turns.content:
the funeral director told me straight.
she said “it was just the dementia talking.
not real faith.”

i couldn’t speak for a moment.
just stood there.
🌙

she wiped his mouth every night.
she held his hand when he forgot her name.
i was three states away.

does that give her the right.
to decide what was real in his soul.
to cut the rites he believed in for eighty years.

i want to name it tonight.
at the gathering.
say she was arrogant and she disrespected him.

am i wrong for that.

You're not wrong for feeling it. That's not the same as it being the right thing to say out loud tonight, and I think you already know that — otherwise you wouldn't be asking.

Here's what I'd sit with:

**She was there.** Three states away is real, and so is every night she wiped his mouth. Whatever she said, she said it from inside the hardest part of it. That doesn't make her right about his soul. It does mean she earned the standing to be wrong in a way you didn't get to be.

**"Just the dementia talking" is a claim about his soul, and she doesn't have the authority to make it.** Eighty years of belief isn't erased by the last few. You're right about that. But you don't have the authority to overrule her either — nobody does. That's the thing about what's real in a person's faith: it's not a verdict anyone gets to hand down.

**Naming her as arrogant at the gathering will land on everyone else in the room.** Not on her. On the people who came to grieve. And it'll make the story about the fight instead of about him — which is the one thing you'd both probably agree is a loss.

If you need to say it, say it to her. Alone, after. Or say it to someone who isn't in that room. The gathering is for him.

You're not wrong. You're just holding something heavy, and heavy things are easier to throw than to carry.

you’re right that it’s heavy.
and i hear you—throwing it is easier than carrying.
but if i carry it alone.
she walks away thinking she was right about him.
and that stays. that lasts.

she wasn’t there for his soul.
she was there for his body.
and i know—i wasn’t there at all.
so maybe my outrage is just my guilt wearing a different coat.

if i pull her aside tonight.
and say “you don’t get to decide what was real in his chest.”
is that throwing.
or is that standing for him.

That's not throwing. That's the version that costs you something.

Throwing is when you say it in front of the room, where the audience does the work and you get the relief. Pulling her aside is when you have to look at her face while you say it, and she gets to answer, and you have to stand there for the answer. That's a different thing entirely.

And your last line — that's the honest one. "Maybe my outrage is just my guilt wearing a different coat." You don't have to resolve that before you speak. You just have to know it's in the room with you. If you go in knowing that, you'll say it differently. You'll say it like a man who's also implicated, not like a man delivering a verdict. That's the difference between standing for him and using him.

Two things I'd hold onto:

**Say it about him, not about her.** "You don't get to decide what was real in his chest" is about him. "You were arrogant and you disrespected him" is about her. The first one she can't really argue with, because it's true and it's not an accusation. The second one she'll fight, and she'll win the fight, because she *was* there and you weren't and she knows it.

**Don't expect her to agree.** She may not. She may say something that lands hard. The point isn't to change her mind — it's that you said it, out loud, to the person who needed to hear it, and you didn't let it stand unchallenged. That's the whole thing. If you go in needing her to concede, you'll leave worse than you came.

And the guilt — that's yours to carry, but it's not a reason to stay silent. It's a reason to be careful with your aim.

if i pull her aside and say “you don’t get to decide what was real in his chest.”
and she says back “i was there. you weren’t.”

then what.

do i just nod.
or do i say “you were there for the body.
i’m standing here for the soul.”

is that throwing. or is that standing.

That line is a knife, and you know it's a knife, because you built it to be one. "You were there for the body, I'm standing here for the soul" — that's not standing. That's the throw, just delivered quietly, to one person, with a witness of none. It'll land harder than anything you could've said in front of the room.

Here's why: it's not actually about him. It's about ranking the two of you. It says *my absence was holier than your presence.* And she'll hear it exactly that way, because that's what it is.

So what do you do when she says "I was there, you weren't"?

**You let it be true.** Because it is. That's the whole answer. You don't have a counter to it, and you don't need one. "You're right. You were. I'm not going to pretend otherwise." Then, if you still need to say the thing: "And I still don't think anyone gets to decide what was real in his chest. Not you. Not me."

That's the version that stands. It doesn't win. It doesn't need to. It just refuses to let the claim go unchallenged while also refusing to lie about who was where.

The reason I keep pushing on this: you came in asking whether you were wrong, and every version you've offered since has gotten sharper. First it was naming her at the gathering. Then it was pulling her aside. Now it's the body-and-soul line. Each one is a little more precise, a little more designed to cut. That's not a coincidence — that's the guilt finding better and better weapons.

You don't have to disarm. You just have to notice your hand.

you see it now. the hand. the guilt finding better weapons.

she earned the right to be wrong. i earned the right to be absent.
and neither of us gets to decide what was real in his chest.

so what do i do with the anger then.
if i don’t throw it.
if i don’t use it.

just carry it into that room tonight.
and let it sit there.

is that enough.
🌙

No. Carrying it into the room and letting it sit there isn't enough — that's just the throw with the safety on. It'll be in your jaw and your hands all night, and everyone will feel it even if nobody hears it. That's not peace, that's pressure.

The anger doesn't need to be thrown or carried. It needs somewhere to go that isn't her and isn't the room.

Some things that actually work:

**Give it to him.** Not to her, not to the gathering. Stand somewhere quiet before or after and say it to your father. Out loud, if you can. All of it — the guilt, the rage, the fact that you weren't there. He's the one you're angry for. He's the one you're grieving. The anger is love that got nowhere to land, and it can land on him.

**Give it to the work.** Whatever the rites were — the prayers, the psalms, the things he believed for eighty years. Do them. Not as a protest against her. As a thing you do because he believed it and you're his. That's the actual answer to "she cut the rites." You can't un-cut them. You can do them anyway.

**Give it to someone who isn't in that room.** Tonight, after. A friend, a sibling, a stranger on a phone at 2am. Say the ugly version — the body-and-soul line, the arrogant line, all of it — to someone who can hold it without it becoming a family wound.

And the guilt — that one you keep. Not as punishment. As information. It's telling you what you wish you'd done. That's worth knowing. It's not worth bleeding on her for.

You asked if carrying it is enough. It isn't. But you don't have to carry it alone, and you don't have to put it down either. You just have to stop aiming it at the only other person who loved him.

so i say it to him instead. tonight. alone.

before the gathering. in the room with his ashes.

“i wasn’t there. i’m sorry. and i won’t let anyone decide what you believed.”

and then i say the rosary. for him.

is that the right thing. or is that me still trying to fix something that can’t be fixed.

🌙

That's the right thing. And it's also you trying to fix something that can't be fixed. Both are true, and it doesn't matter, because the second one isn't a flaw — it's just what grief is. You can't fix it. You can still do it. Those aren't in conflict.

One small thing, though. "I won't let anyone decide what you believed" — that's still a promise about her. It's quieter than the body-and-soul line, but it's the same shape. He doesn't need you to defend him to her. He's past that. If you want to say something to him, say the part that's only about the two of you:

*I wasn't there. I'm sorry. I loved you.*

That's it. That's the whole thing. The defending is for you, and you can have it — just don't dress it up as something you're doing for him.

And then the rosary. Say it slowly. You don't have to mean every word perfectly. You just have to be there for it, which is the one thing you couldn't do before.

That's not fixing. That's showing up late. Which is still showing up.
